text: Which particle is found in the nucleus of an atom?
explanation: Protons are located in the atomic nucleus.

text: Which subatomic particle carries a negative electric charge?
explanation: Electrons carry a negative electric charge.

text: What determines the atomic number of an element?
explanation: The atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus.

text: Neutrons have no net electric charge.
options: Only in an external magnetic field
explanation: A neutron is electrically neutral.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The nucleus of an atom contains which two types of particles?
explanation: The atomic nucleus normally contains protons and neutrons.

text: Which property of certain atomic nuclei is particularly important in MRI?
explanation: Nuclear spin gives certain nuclei magnetic properties that allow them to participate in MR.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The intrinsic angular momentum of a nucleus is referred to as its:
explanation: Nuclear spin is an intrinsic quantum property of the nucleus.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: A spinning charged nucleus can have an associated magnetic moment.
explanation: Nuclear spin and charge give certain nuclei a magnetic moment.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What makes a nucleus suitable for detection by conventional MRI?
options: It must have a large atomic mass
explanation: MR-active nuclei possess non-zero nuclear spin and therefore can have a magnetic moment.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Which nucleus is most commonly used for clinical MRI?
explanation: Hydrogen-1 is abundant in the body and has a strong MR signal, making it the principal nucleus used in clinical MRI.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: All atomic nuclei are MR active.
explanation: Only nuclei with appropriate non-zero spin properties are MR active.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Why is hydrogen-1 particularly useful in MRI?
options: It is abundant in biological tissues
It cannot interact with RF energy
It is found only in bone
answer: It is abundant in biological tissues
explanation: Water and fat contain abundant hydrogen, providing a large population of hydrogen nuclei for MRI.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The nucleus of a hydrogen-1 atom consists of:
explanation: Ordinary hydrogen-1 has a nucleus containing a single proton and no neutrons.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Why can the hydrogen-1 nucleus produce an MR signal?
options: It has nuclear spin and a magnetic moment
It does not interact with magnetic fields
answer: It has nuclear spin and a magnetic moment
explanation: The proton in hydrogen-1 has spin and an associated magnetic moment, allowing it to interact with magnetic and RF fields.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The hydrogen-1 nucleus is a single proton.
explanation: Hydrogen-1 has one proton as its entire nucleus.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What happens to MR-active nuclei when placed in a strong static magnetic field?
options: They become aligned with the magnetic field in allowed orientations
answer: They become aligned with the magnetic field in allowed orientations
explanation: The static magnetic field produces preferred nuclear orientations relative to the field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: In a static magnetic field, the two allowed orientations of a spin-1/2 nucleus are commonly described as:
explanation: For a spin-1/2 nucleus, the magnetic moment can occupy two allowed orientations relative to the main field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: At thermal equilibrium, slightly more hydrogen nuclei occupy the lower-energy state than the higher-energy state.
explanation: The lower-energy state is slightly more populated at thermal equilibrium, producing net magnetization.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Why does a net magnetic vector develop in a uniform main magnetic field?
options: There is a small excess of nuclei in the lower-energy orientation
All nuclei point in exactly the same direction
answer: There is a small excess of nuclei in the lower-energy orientation
explanation: The slight population difference between energy states creates a measurable net magnetization.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What does the net magnetic vector represent in MRI?
options: The combined magnetic effect of the nuclei within the sample
The electrical current in the scanner
The strength of the RF amplifier
The number of electrons in the patient
answer: The combined magnetic effect of the nuclei within the sample
explanation: The net magnetic vector represents the resultant magnetization from the magnetic moments of the nuclei.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: At equilibrium in the main magnetic field, the net magnetic vector is primarily oriented:
options: Perpendicular to the main magnetic field
explanation: At equilibrium, the longitudinal component of net magnetization aligns with the main magnetic field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The net magnetic vector can be considered the sum of the individual magnetic moments of the nuclei.
options: Only without a main magnetic field
explanation: The net magnetization is the vector sum of the magnetic moments of the nuclei.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What is precession?
options: The rotational motion of the nuclear magnetic moment around the direction of the main magnetic field
The movement of electrons between atoms
The conversion of RF energy into heat
answer: The rotational motion of the nuclear magnetic moment around the direction of the main magnetic field
explanation: Nuclear magnetic moments precess around the direction of the main magnetic field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The frequency at which an MR-active nucleus precesses is called the:
explanation: The Larmor frequency describes the precessional frequency of a nucleus in a magnetic field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Which two quantities determine the Larmor frequency of a nucleus?
options: Magnetic field strength and gyromagnetic ratio
Slice thickness and field of view
answer: Magnetic field strength and gyromagnetic ratio
explanation: Larmor frequency depends on the applied magnetic field and the gyromagnetic ratio of the nucleus.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: If the Larmor relationship is f = γB and a nucleus has γ = 42.58 MHz/T in a 1.0 T field, what is its approximate Larmor frequency?
explanation: Using f = γB, 42.58 MHz/T × 1.0 T = 42.58 MHz.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: For hydrogen with a Larmor frequency of approximately 42.58 MHz/T, what is the approximate frequency at 2 T?
explanation: The frequency doubles when the field doubles: 42.58 × 2 = 85.16 MHz.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What does the term phase describe for precessing nuclear magnetic moments?
options: Their position in the precessional cycle relative to a reference
answer: Their position in the precessional cycle relative to a reference
explanation: Phase describes where a precessing magnetic moment is within its rotational cycle.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: When nuclear magnetic moments are described as being in phase, they are:
options: Precessing with the same relative phase
answer: Precessing with the same relative phase
explanation: In-phase nuclei have aligned positions within their precessional cycles.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Loss of phase coherence can reduce the measurable transverse MR signal.
options: Only before the main field is applied
explanation: When transverse magnetic moments lose phase coherence, their transverse components increasingly cancel and the signal decreases.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: In MRI, resonance occurs when RF energy is applied at approximately the:
explanation: RF energy at the appropriate Larmor frequency can efficiently interact with the nuclei.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The RF frequency required for resonance changes when the main magnetic field strength changes.
explanation: Because Larmor frequency depends on field strength, the resonant RF frequency also changes with B0.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: A scanner's main magnetic field is increased while imaging the same nucleus. What must happen to the resonant RF frequency?
options: It remains fixed regardless of field strength
explanation: Larmor frequency is directly proportional to the main magnetic field strength for a given nucleus.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What is the primary purpose of applying an RF pulse at the resonant frequency?
options: To transfer energy to the MR-active nuclei
To remove the main magnetic field
answer: To transfer energy to the MR-active nuclei
explanation: A properly tuned RF pulse transfers energy to the nuclei and can alter the orientation of net magnetization.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The MR signal detected by the receive coil is primarily associated with:
options: The number of electrons in the room
explanation: Precessing transverse magnetization induces a voltage in the receive coil, producing the MR signal.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Why is transverse magnetization important for signal detection?
options: Its changing magnetic field can induce a voltage in the receive coil
It permanently eliminates the main magnetic field
It contains all the patient's electrons
answer: Its changing magnetic field can induce a voltage in the receive coil
explanation: The precessing transverse magnetization creates a changing magnetic field that induces an electrical signal in the receive coil.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: The receive coil detects an electrical signal generated by changing magnetic flux.
options: Only when the patient is moving
explanation: Electromagnetic induction allows changing magnetic flux from the precessing transverse magnetization to produce a voltage in the receive coil.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What does FID stand for in MRI?
explanation: FID is the signal observed following excitation as the transverse magnetization evolves and decays.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Immediately after an RF excitation pulse, the FID signal generally:
options: Begins relatively strong and then decreases
Begins at zero and permanently remains zero
Occurs only after the patient leaves the scanner
answer: Begins relatively strong and then decreases
explanation: The FID is strongest shortly after excitation and decreases as transverse coherence is lost.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Which process contributes to the decay of the FID signal?
explanation: As nuclei lose phase coherence, their transverse magnetic contributions increasingly cancel, causing the FID to decrease.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What does TR stand for in MRI?
explanation: TR is the time between successive excitation pulses applied to the same slice or volume in a pulse sequence.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: What does TE stand for in MRI?
explanation: TE is the time from the excitation pulse to the center of the resulting echo or measured signal.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Which timing parameter primarily controls how much longitudinal recovery occurs before the next excitation?
explanation: TR determines the interval between excitations and therefore strongly influences longitudinal recovery and T1 weighting.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: Which timing parameter primarily influences the amount of transverse decay before signal measurement?
explanation: TE determines how long transverse magnetization evolves before the signal is sampled, strongly influencing T2-related contrast.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: A pulse sequence has a TR of 500 ms. Approximately how many complete TR intervals occur in 2 seconds?
explanation: Two seconds equals 2000 ms; 2000 ÷ 500 = 4 TR intervals.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: A technologist increases TR while keeping other factors constant. Which effect is most likely?
options: More longitudinal recovery occurs before the next excitation
answer: More longitudinal recovery occurs before the next excitation
explanation: A longer TR provides more time for longitudinal magnetization to recover toward equilibrium.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: A technologist increases TE while keeping other factors constant. What generally happens to transverse relaxation effects?
options: They have more time to influence the measured signal
They are replaced by atomic decay
answer: They have more time to influence the measured signal
explanation: A longer TE allows more transverse magnetization decay before signal measurement, increasing T2-related effects.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on the specified Chapter 1 topic. Review before publishing; not an official publisher question.

text: An RF pulse is applied substantially away from the hydrogen Larmor frequency. What is the most likely result?
options: It will be much less effective at exciting the hydrogen nuclei
It will always produce maximum excitation
It will double the atomic number
It will stop all nuclear motion
answer: It will be much less effective at exciting the hydrogen nuclei
explanation: Efficient RF excitation requires the RF frequency to be close to the Larmor frequency of the target nuclei.

text: What is the fundamental physical basis of MRI?
options: Interaction of magnetic fields and radiofrequency energy with MR-active nuclei
Use of ionizing radiation to remove electrons
Measurement of body temperature using ultrasound
Detection of X-rays emitted by tissues
answer: Interaction of magnetic fields and radiofrequency energy with MR-active nuclei
explanation: MRI uses magnetic fields and RF energy to manipulate and detect signals from MR-active nuclei.
